Text & colour

Editorial policy

Philosophy Defined is a curated archive. Selection, wording, and attribution are editorial judgments accountable to evidence.

Last updated: 30 September 2026. The archive holds 696 passages: 57 with the original wording recorded, 1 edition-checked only, 152 annotated, 486 recorded only.

Purpose

The archive presents sourced English philosophy quotations for reading, teaching, and reflection. It is not a substitute for primary texts, scholarly editions, or peer-reviewed commentary.

Coverage

The curated set spans 696 passages drawn from Greco-Roman, Chinese, Indian, Islamic, Jewish, Japanese, and Africana traditions, with expanded representation of women philosophers. Coverage aims at balanced depth rather than an exhaustive canon.

Selection criteria

Passages are included when they are attributable with reasonable confidence, philosophically substantive, and clear in English. We exclude political slogans without philosophical content, viral misattributions, and opaque jargon that cannot be responsibly rendered.

Attribution standard

Each entry records thinker, school, source, and theme. Where scholarly debate exists about authorship or wording, we prefer the most widely recognized attribution and note uncertainty in source fields when needed. Famous lines are not kept merely because they are famous if the attribution is known to be false.

Verification levels

Every quotation page states its level, and the levels mean the same thing everywhere on the site — the homepage, the About page, and each passage's status line read one shared register:

  • Original text checked. Checked against the cited edition, and the wording in the author's own language recorded beside the English.
  • Edition checked. Checked against the cited edition, with the circulating variants and the attribution note; no original-language text is recorded in the register yet.
  • Annotated. A source locator plus commentary written for the passage; the wording has not yet been collated against an edition.
  • Recorded. The English wording and the source as the corpus records them; not yet collated, and kept out of search results until the page carries writing of its own.

Recorded pages carry the corpus wording and source but nothing checked, so they say so and are marked noindex until they carry writing of their own. “Verified” without a level attached is not used anywhere on the site.

English renderings

Primary display language is English. Renderings are checked against reliable published translations and reference works. We do not invent classical-language wording for display. Where multiple reputable English versions exist, we choose clarity for general readers while preserving philosophical sense.

Corrections

If an attribution, theme label, or wording is wrong, we correct it and retain the entry when the passage remains suitable. Removed entries are those that fail the selection criteria after review. Duplicate entries for the same passage are merged, and the old address redirects to the surviving page. Report an error to kyreemeng@gmail.com.

Corrections log

  • 2026-09-27 · /quotes/q0112 — Nietzsche, “One must still have chaos in oneself…”: locator corrected from Zarathustra Part I, “On the Way of the Creator,” to the Prologue, §5.
  • 2026-09-27 · /quotes/q0450 — Nietzsche, “Was that life? Well then! Once more!”: previously a paraphrase attributed to The Gay Science §341. Replaced with the verbatim line and its source, Zarathustra Part III, “On the Vision and the Riddle,” §1.
  • 2026-09-27 · /quotes/q0222 — Plato, “First, it always is, and neither comes to be nor perishes”: Stephanus locator corrected from Symposium 211b to 211a.
  • 2026-09-27 · /quotes/q0070 — Nietzsche, “What does not kill me makes me stronger”: a second entry for the same aphorism (formerly Q0426) was merged into this one, which records the short form as a circulating variant.

Independence

Editorial decisions are not sold. Affiliate or advertising relationships, if introduced later, will be disclosed and will not determine which quotations appear in the archive.
